apps.localizedDescription:
MuffinEMU is a Wii U emulator for iPhone and iPad, iOS 15 and later, built on Cemu: PowerPC interpreters, an AArch64 recompiler, Cafe OS HLE and a native Metal renderer under a SwiftUI app with a measured Wii U GamePad layout. Some MeloCafe cores and bug fixes have been brought over to MuffinEMU.

This source serves the ad-hoc signed build for TrollStore and jailbroken devices, with the JIT entitlements embedded so the recompiler can get executable memory. On SideStore or AltStore use the standard source instead - those re-sign at install and would strip these entitlements.

Bring your own games and keys. No copyrighted content is distributed here.

Three fixes to the on-screen controls, none of them confirmed on a device yet. If
the d-pad still does nothing after this, the two new things below are what to
check, and they will say which half of the chain is at fault.

### Buttons that were dead stay dead, even across updates

MuffinEMU saves a controller profile on your device. If that file lost the
bindings for some buttons, those buttons do nothing - and because the damage is
in a file rather than in the app, reinstalling and updating never fixed it. The
sticks kept working throughout, which made it look like the pad was half broken.

There was already a repair for this, but it only asked whether A or B still had a
binding and took that as proof the whole profile was fine. A profile can lose the
d-pad and keep A and B, and that is exactly what it did: the check passed, the
repair never ran. It now checks every GamePad button, and fills in only the ones
that have nothing bound, so anything you remapped yourself is left alone.

**Settings > On-screen Controls > Reset controller bindings** is new. It wipes the
saved profile and rebuilds the defaults, and tells you how many bindings you
ended up with rather than just claiming success. Use it if some buttons do
nothing while the sticks still work.

### A finger resting on a button while a game started could kill it for the session

The emulator takes a reading of the controller the first time a game asks for
input and treats whatever it sees as the controller's resting posi...

Superseded by 4.1, which adds a third controls fix on top of these two. Install
4.1 instead.

- Repairs a saved controller profile that has lost the bindings for only some
  buttons. The existing repair checked whether A or B still had a binding and
  took that as proof the profile was intact, so a profile that had lost the
  d-pad and kept A and B was passed through untouched. Adds
  **Settings > On-screen Controls > Reset controller bindings**.
- Melo-Controller's size slider now resizes each button in place instead of
  scaling the whole pad, which used to push the outer buttons off the screen.

## The pad is now Muffin Classic's, plus 79 deliberate lines

**Install this one.** Rather than keep repairing a diverged copy, the on-screen pad is now
the same code as the original Muffin app - whose controls have always worked - with a short,
named list of additions on top. **378 lines of MuffinEMU-only machinery are gone.**

That turned out to be a cheap trade. A file-by-file comparison of every control-related
source showed `ControllerSkins`, `ControllerSkinPalette`, `ControllerSkinsLibrary`,
`ControllerSkinSelectorByCategory`, `GamePadGeometry` and `MuffinPadCustomisation` were
**already byte-identical** between the two apps. Only two features in the whole pad were
MuffinEMU-only: comfort controls and haptics. Everything else was machinery wrapped around a
press path that worked fine in its simpler form.

### Removed

`DpadTouchSurface` and the `dpadHeld` state it needed. The four directions go back to being
ordinary controls, as in Classic. That also removes `externallyPressed`, which existed only
so that surface could drive a button's drawn state from outside.

### Kept

- **Comfort controls** - four cluster choices and one setting. Pure layout; it never touches
  the press path.
- The safety nets for edit mode switching on under a finger, and for the app resigning
  active - both cases where the system cancels a gesture without a guaranteed release and a
  control would otherwise stay stuck ...

## Correction, added after publishing

**The explanation below is now in doubt, and the honest thing is to say so at the top.**

A later comparison against the ORIGINAL Muffin app - whose on-screen controls have always
worked - found that it contains the *identical* guard:

    guard isPressed != value else { return }

Same line, same place, working fine. So the guard alone cannot be the cause, and the
confident claim below that it "was" the bug is wrong.

What this release actually does is make the report to the engine unable to desync at all,
which is a real robustness improvement and may well fix the symptom - but the mechanism is
NOT confirmed, and this is the fifth explanation offered for this bug. Treat it as "worth
installing and testing", not as "solved".

What genuinely differs between the two pads, and is the better place to keep looking:
MuffinEMU's version adds a shared `DpadTouchSurface`, a `dpadHeld` @State set on the
cluster that every button's parameters now read, plus `isInteractive`, `externallyPressed`
and `isPaused` - none of which exist in the original. Skins, geometry and pad customisation
are byte-identical between the two.

## The original explanation, kept for the record

**Install this one.** After five attempts, this was believed to be the first with a
mechanism explaining every observation.

**Use this one, not 3.6.** Same diagnostic build, but the d-pad is instrumented too. In 3.6
the touch counter was wired only into face buttons - the d-pad has its own separate gesture
and would not have been counted, which is half of what is reported broken.

## Still a diagnostic build, not a fix

Buttons remain broken and this does not claim to fix them. Four theories have now been
shipped for this bug - touch slop, the preview pad, a stale controller profile, missing
button mappings - and the symptom outlived all of them. Rather than guess a fifth time, this
build buys a measurement.

The fact that narrowed it: **the buttons show no press animation.** That animation is driven
by `isPressed` inside `HeldControl`, flipped only by its own `DragGesture` - so no animation
means the gesture never fired, which means touches are not reaching the buttons at all. A
touch-DELIVERY problem in the UI layer, not an emulator or bridge one. The sticks keep
working because they are a different view type with their own gesture.

A fresh review of the code, done without sight of the earlier theories, independently
confirmed that every controller file is byte-identical to a commit where buttons worked,
that the pad sits on top of everything hit-testable in the default play state, and that no
competing gesture is attached. It found no provable cause in the source - and said so
rather than inventing one.

## Dead buttons: root cause found and fixed

**Install this if your on-screen buttons stopped working.**

The clue that cracked it was that **the joysticks still responded**. That single detail rules
out everything the previous four releases tried: if sticks work, touches ARE reaching the
pad, the pad IS mounted, and hit testing is fine. Every layout, touch-slop and
`contentShape` theory was wrong.

The asymmetry is architectural. In `GCController.mm`:

    btn(kBitA, 0);                    // buttons -> raw INDICES, need a mapping table
    result.axis.x = s.leftStick.x;    // axes    -> straight through, no mapping

Axes reach the emulated controller directly and never consult the mapping table. Every
button goes through it. So **"sticks respond, no button does" is the exact signature of an
emulated controller with no button mappings** - and nothing in the app said so.

Why it had none: the default mappings were applied **only when a new emulated controller
was created**. A profile persisted in `controllerProfiles/controller{N}` is loaded at
startup, so that branch was skipped - and a profile carrying no usable button bindings left
every button dead, on every launch, on every future build.

**That is also why v3.4 did not help.** The bad state was DATA on the device, not code in
the binary. Restoring the input path byte-for-byte - which v3.4 did, and which was verified
against a known-good state - ...

## This release exists to get on-screen buttons working again

**Install this one if pad buttons stopped responding.** It is the first build with every
suspect removed at once.

### The whole input path is back to a known-good state

Every file the on-screen pad depends on is now **byte-identical** to the last state with
confirmed working buttons (2026-09-14 17:19):

    ControllerPad.swift          ControllerLayout.swift
    ControllerCustomLayout.swift MeloControls.swift
    GamePadGeometry.swift        ControllerSkins.swift

Also verified unchanged against that state: the bridge's input path (`set_button_state`,
the input mutex, stick axes) and the pad's call site in `ContentView`.

### What was removed

**v3.3's touch-slop change - mine, and it broke all pad input.** It widened each button's
tap target with the usual SwiftUI idiom: `padding` -> `contentShape` -> negative `padding`.
That idiom is correct in a stack and **wrong under `.position()`**, which is how every pad
control is placed. Negative padding reports a layout frame *smaller* than the content, hit
testing clips to that frame, and the result is a catchment smaller than the button - zero
for anything under about 16pt. Nothing looks wrong; the buttons simply stop answering.

The "Button responsiveness" slider and "Animate presses" toggle are gone with it. A second,
different implementation was written and deliberately **not** shipped - ...

MuffinEMU, Wii U emulation for iPhone and iPad, built from commit aac1260a.

Everything from **v3.2** carries over - the Single Screen sizing fix, Low Power Mode, the
automatic cool-down and the heat readout, the two appearance switches. This release adds
the on-screen controls work.

## Pad presses now animate

Buttons dip under your finger and spring back. The timing is asymmetric on purpose: the
press is a 45ms ease-out, the release is a spring. A spring on the way *down* would make a
button that registered at touch-down **look** like it registered late, which is the exact
complaint this is meant to answer.

Honours Reduce Motion, and there is an **Animate presses** toggle if you would rather they
snap. Nothing about how a control looks at rest has changed.

## Button responsiveness is now a slider

Settings > On-screen Controls. Worth being precise about what it does, rather than shipping
a mystery dial:

**Nothing in the input path delays a press.** The pad reports on `DragGesture`'s `onChanged`
- the first moment a touch exists - and there is no timer anywhere to shorten. A button that
"did not respond" was almost never late. The finger landed just off it, or slid off it
mid-press.

So the slider widens the *target* instead of speeding up a clock that is already instant:
**0-20pt of invisible catchment** outside each button's painted edge. The button looks
identical at every setting; only the area that accepts a touch changes. The row shows the

## The big one: Single Screen rendered tiny in the corner

Fixed, and it had been there since **v1.0**. `MetalLayerHandle`'s constructor measured
CoreAnimation's current drawable size off the layer and made the implied scale
authoritative. By the time it ran, that number was wrong: the bridge sets the layer's
`contentsScale` to your Render Scale (**Balanced is the default and is half native**), then
the render view enters a window and **UIKit re-asserts the screen's scale**, so the drawable
came out twice the linear size the engine thought the window was. The image was drawn into
the top-left quarter and the rest was cleared black.

Only Single Screen, because the two-screen layouts change size when the layout resolves and
repair it by accident. The fix reads the scale the bridge already wrote instead of measuring
the layer.

**Not yet confirmed on a device.** A free check that confirms or kills it: set Render Scale
to Native and relaunch. If the picture fills the screen there and gets *smaller* on Battery
saver, the diagnosis is right.

## Reverted: the L3/R3 hit-target change from v2.6

Reported as making on-screen control responsiveness dramatically worse (a
~1.5-2 second hold needed to register at all) - a far more severe problem than
the narrow diagonal-vs-L3 issue it was trying to fix. Every control, L3/R3
included, is back to the same square hit-region they always had before v2.6.

## Single Screen sizing: third attempt, reverted to literally no extra logic

Two rounds of computed sizing math for the single-screen case were both
reported as making the picture render incorrectly on real hardware. The
original (pre-MeloCafe-port) Muffin app's own shipped code for this exact
situation carried no frame or position math at all - this now matches that
exactly.

## Fixed: TV picture confined to a corner instead of filling the screen

Root-caused this time from an actual device log rather than another guess. The
registered surface was correctly "1366x1024 points, 1.0x scale" - that's Render
Scale: Balanced (the default), deliberately rendering at half native resolution
on a 2x-scale display to save GPU/battery, which is intentional and correct on
its own. The real bug: the code that resizes the Metal drawable to match that
reduced scale never updated the layer's `contentsScale` to match it - so a
Retina layer's `contentsScale` (frozen at native 2x from once-at-startup setup)
disagreed with its own drawable's actual pixel density, and iOS displayed that
drawable at its own native pixel size instead of stretching it to fill the
screen. This was very likely present since long before th...

## Fixed: Single Screen / Adaptive rendering tiny in the top-left corner

v2.3's Screen Layout port left the emulated screen rendering small, pinned to the
top-left corner, instead of fullscreen - present from the very first launch, not
just after swapping. Root cause: the view showing the TV/GamePad screen is a raw
UIKit view wrapped for SwiftUI, and `.frame(maxWidth: .infinity, maxHeight: .infinity)`
doesn't reliably force a view like that to actually fill the space SwiftUI gives it,
unlike a native SwiftUI view. MeloCafe's own equivalent avoids this by wrapping its
view in an inner `GeometryReader` and applying an explicit, measured size instead of
a flexible one - that wrapper was missing here and is now in place. The emulated
screen fills the same space the on-screen GamePad buttons already span.
